t.5.4.1: Then the wise one saw in the sky the radiant one, the moon, which had reached the middle of the heavens and was pouring forth a vast canopy of moonlight. Shining brightly, it roamed like a maddened bull wandering in a cow-pen.
t.5.4.3: The splendor that shines on earth when it rests upon Mount Mandara, and likewise upon the ocean in the evenings, and likewise upon the waters when it dwells in the lotus, that same splendor shone forth resting in the lovely moon.
t.5.4.2: Then he saw the cool-rayed moon rising, destroying the sins of the world, swelling the great ocean, and making all beings shine.
t.5.4.4: Like a swan dwelling in a silver cage, like a lion dwelling in a cave of Mount Mandara, like a hero mounted on a proud elephant, so too the moon shone, dwelling in the sky.
t.5.4.5: The moon, its horns at the full, shines forth: it stands like a bull with sharp horns, like the great mountain Śveta with its lofty peaks, like an elephant whose tusks are bound with gold.
t.5.4.6: The blessed evening shone like heaven: its darkness was dispelled by the rising of the bright moon, the wickedness of the flesh-eating rākṣasas grew strong, and the sulking hearts of lovely women were soothed by their charming lovers.
t.5.4.8: The wise monkey beheld the mansions, thronged with the drunken and the heedless, crowded with chariots, horses and splendid seats, and filled as well with the glory of heroes.
t.5.4.7: The sounds of stringed instruments, pleasing to the ear, have begun; virtuous women sleep beside their husbands; and the night-roamers too, of most wondrous and fierce conduct, have likewise set forth to sport.
t.5.4.9: They taunt one another excessively and fling about their brawny arms; they pour forth drunken ravings, and the intoxicated ones revile one another.
t.5.4.10: He saw Rākṣasas thrusting out their chests and flinging their limbs upon their beloveds; he saw beloved women talking together, while others there were sleeping again.
t.5.4.11: The city shone with great trumpeting elephants, with well-honored and virtuous people, and with heroes breathing heavily, as a lake shines with hissing serpents.
t.5.4.12: In that city he saw yātudhānas who were foremost in intelligence and pleasing in speech, full of faith and foremost in the world, of many different kinds and bearing charming names.
t.5.4.13: He rejoiced on seeing those handsome beings, endowed with various qualities and true to their own natures, shining with splendour. He saw those handsome ones, and then again some who were misshapen.
t.5.4.14: Then he saw there their women, worthy of the best, of utterly pure disposition and great dignity, whose hearts were also set on delightful drinks, shining like brilliant stars.
t.5.4.15: At midnight he saw some women blazing with splendour yet wrapped in modesty, held in their lovers' embrace and enfolded in delight, like birds nestled among flowers.
t.5.4.16: The wise one saw still other women seated on the rooftop terraces, sitting at ease there in the laps of their beloveds; dear to their husbands and devoted to dharma, they remained settled there, possessed by love.
t.5.4.17: He saw women, some unveiled and gleaming like streaks of gold, some of surpassing beauty with the hue of refined gold, and others again with the colour of the hare-marked moon, women of lovely limbs and complexion, parted from their beloveds.
t.5.4.18: Then, looking carefully about, that foremost hero among the monkeys saw in the houses exceedingly lovely women, joyful and filled with deep affection, who had gained their dear lovers, delightful to the heart.
t.5.4.19: He saw rows of faces shining like the moon, rows of lovely eyes with curving lashes, and rows of ornaments gleaming like beautiful garlands of lightning.
t.5.4.20: But nowhere did he see Sītā, of supremely noble birth, born into a royal house that stood firm on the righteous path, slender, noble in mind, and fair like a well-grown creeper in full bloom.
t.5.4.21: Her who was firmly set upon the eternal path, whose eyes were turned toward Rāma, who was possessed by love, who had entered into the glorious mind of her husband, and who was ever distinguished above all women, even the most excellent.
t.5.4.23: He saw her like a crescent moon whose outline is faint, like a streak of gold smeared with dust, like the line of an arrow-wound grown over after the hurt, like a streak of cloud torn apart by the wind.
t.5.4.24: Not seeing Sītā, the wife of Rāma, lord of men and best of speakers, the monkey, after so long a time, was struck down by grief and at once became as though downcast.
t.5.4.22: Her, tormented by heat, her throat streaming with tears, whose neck was once adorned with the finest and most precious gold ornaments; her of lovely eyelashes and sweet-sounding voice, like a peahen wandering in the forest.
